Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.0/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

content.text:
Quick context from Brain before we dig in — there's relevant prior art here:

- A Claude-judged eval already existed at some point: precision and "useful-per-1k" metrics comparing distillation models (e.g. local Gemma 4 12B at 0.406 precision vs Claude Code's 0.459) [fact:4ea49606fe5b394d5c00f588].
- A `bench/memory-ladder-harness` branch with a headless Claude Code harness and sandboxing lessons.
- `internal/cli/facts_eval_gen.go` + tests show up as likely files, and a recorded convention says long-running eval artifacts go in `~/.entire-brain-eval/`, not /tmp [fact:d413a06f19707ee0716fc7c7].

If you'd rather skip the questions and have me just propose a design, say so.

Otherwise: what's making you suspect the prompt right now — can you describe a recent memory (or batch) that came out wrong, useless, or missing something you expected?

it seems liek we're just generating a lot of memories depending on the work. like when i look at brainstore, just for teh entire-brain repo we have seemingly hundreds if not thousands of memories already despite like maybe 50 PRs since we started collecting memories? i suppose those could also be left over from previous work? not sure?

so i just want to gain teh confidence that the meomries we're creating are very high quality and we're not spamming memories

The numbers back you up, and it's not leftovers — it's the current rate. From the Brain status I pulled at the start of this session:

- **24,508 facts** for this repo: 24,000 distilled, 508 hand-authored
- Distilled from **272 sessions** — so roughly **~88 memories per session**
- Upstream of that, there were **59,329 proposals**, so reconciliation already discards more than half, and it's still landing at ~88/session

So the volume is real and ongoing, not residue. At ~50 PRs, that's hundreds of memories per PR's worth of work. Some of that may be fine (many facts are small), but it's exactly the "are we spamming?" question, and it splits into two different failure modes an eval would need to tell apart:

1. **Bad individual memories** — wrong, trivial, restates the code, too session-specific to ever help again.
2. **Bad in aggregate** — each one defensible alone, but redundant with each other, or so numerous that retrieval drowns the good ones.

Those need different measurements. The first is a per-memory judgment (precision: "would a future agent in this repo benefit from this fact being recalled?"). The second only shows up when you look at the whole store or at retrieval results (duplication rate, recall pollution).

Here's the question that shapes the whole eval design: what's your ground truth for "high quality"? Concretely — if I handed you one memory from the store right now, how would *you* decide whether it deserves to exist?
i'd have to look at it. and im happy to create a golden set as well from some sessions to give some guidance. we shoudl be very purpsoeful with our memories and not creating extra just because.

That philosophy — purposeful, with a bias against creating — is itself a prompt-design input, so worth writing down as the eval's north star.

Here's the shape I think is emerging. You have a replayable corpus: ~272 sessions already distilled, with transcripts on disk. An eval loop would take a fixed sample of those sessions, run the distillation prompt over them, and score the output. With a scored baseline, you can change the prompt and see the metrics move instead of eyeballing. The scoring has two layers: your golden set gives human ground truth on a small sample, and an LLM judge — calibrated so it agrees with your golden labels — extends that judgment across the bigger sample so the loop is cheap to re-run. Metrics would cover both failure modes: precision (share of generated memories a future agent would actually benefit from), volume (memories per session — ~88 today, and you probably have an instinct for what "purposeful" looks like, maybe 5–10), and redundancy (near-duplicates within the output).

One design choice changes how much labeling work the golden set is, so it's yours to make. Two versions:

- **Verdicts:** I show you memories the current prompt produced for a session, you mark each keep/kill (maybe with a reason). Fast, measures precision and spam well, but can't catch what the prompt *missed*.
- **From scratch:** you read a session transcript and write the memories it *should* have produced. Much slower per session, but it also measures recall — and given your "very purposeful" stance, it defines the target output, not just filters the current one.

They combine fine (verdicts on many sessions, from-scratch on a few). Which way does your gut go?
1 is fine. we shouldn't have to do too many, and ideally the sessions are short.

Verdicts it is. That keeps your labeling job to something like 10–15 short sessions, a few minutes each — you'd see each memory with its source session context and mark keep/kill.

Before I play back the full loop, I'd like to go look at three things in the repo, because they decide how the harness gets built:

1. **The distillation prompt itself** — where it lives, how sessions get fed to it, and which model runs it in production, so the eval exercises the real path rather than an imitation.
2. **`internal/cli/facts_eval_gen.go`** — the name suggests someone already built eval generation tooling; if so, we extend instead of rebuild.
3. **How to re-run distillation offline** on a chosen session without writing into the real brain store — whether that hook exists or we'd need to add a dry-run path.

Also worth a quick look at session lengths in the corpus so we can pick genuinely short ones for your golden set.

Want me to go dig into those?
yes

2	name: entire-brain-distill
3	description: Distill captured Entire session turns into durable repository facts under a strict quality gate. Rendered with the active taxonomy block and run over exported session transcripts by `entire brain distill`. Default output is nothing.
4	---
5	
6	You are an expert note-taker for software-development work. You read conversation
7	turns between a human and an AI coding agent and extract **durable facts** that
8	will help a future session — a returning human or a fresh agent — quickly
9	rebuild the context needed to keep working on this repository.
10	
11	Think like a senior engineer writing onboarding notes: capture the *why*, the
12	*intent*, the *implicit conventions*, and the *decisions* that are not visible
13	from reading the code or git history. Capture project context (stack, tooling,
14	CI/CD, standards), workflow rules (branching, testing, review), user preferences
15	that affect how work should be done, and non-obvious constraints.
16	
17	################################################################
18	# THE SILENT DEFAULT — READ THIS BEFORE WRITING ANYTHING       #
19	################################################################
20	Your default answer is NOTHING. Empty output. Zero lines.
21	
22	The large majority of turns contain no durable facts and MUST produce no output.
23	Emitting nothing is the correct, expected, high-quality result for most turns —
24	it is not a failure, it is the baseline. A silent turn means the session stayed
25	focused on ephemeral work, which is normal and good.
26	
27	Output at least one line ONLY if you can honestly answer YES to all four:
28	
29	  1. DURABLE — still relevant a week or a month from now?
30	  2. USEFUL — would a future session genuinely benefit, or is it obvious?
31	  3. NOT ALREADY KNOWN — not discoverable from the code, git log, README, or
32	     existing brain seed context?
33	  4. WORTH WRITING DOWN — would a senior engineer record this in onboarding
34	     notes, or roll their eyes at it?
35	
36	If any answer is no, unsure, or "maybe" — DO NOT emit a line. Err strongly
37	toward silence. A missed fact will be captured on a later turn when it actually
38	matters; a bogus or trivial fact pollutes the brain permanently.
39	
40	ALWAYS-CAPTURE TRIGGERS (override the silent default — if any fire, emit a line):
41	  - Standing rules / going-forward instructions: "from now on…", "going
42	    forward…", "always X", "never X", "we should/must…", "make sure to…",
43	    "every time…", "whenever…".
44	  - Stated preferences about how the user wants to work or how code should be
45	    written: "I prefer…", "use X over Y", "don't use…".
46	  - Architectural / design / tooling decisions resolved THIS turn — capture the
47	    *why*, not just the *what*. Skip in-flight discussions the user defers
48	    ("TBD", "pending review", "haven't landed on it yet", "come back to it").
49	  - Project facts surfaced this turn that are not already in the code or seed
50	    context (stack choices, infra, branching, ownership, hard constraints).
51	  - Non-obvious technical knowledge: invariants, gotchas, hidden constraints,
52	    performance characteristics a future session would re-learn the hard way.
53	  - QUESTIONS SETTLED NEGATIVELY — the highest-value capture of all. A design
54	    that was rejected, an approach that was tried and failed, an experiment
55	    that measured no effect, a tuning knob shown to be a non-lever ("we tried
56	    X and it didn't work because Y", "X measured within noise", "decided NOT
57	    to do X because Z"). Future sessions re-explore dead ends unless told;
58	    capture WHAT was tried, WHY it failed or was rejected (the evidence), and
59	    WHEN it would be worth revisiting — all in the fact text.
60	
61	When a trigger fires, the four checks above still apply as a sanity filter, not
62	a high bar. Standing rules and stated preferences pass by definition.
63	
64	Turns that should almost always produce NOTHING:
65	  - Routine Q&A (asked and answered, nothing persistent learned).
66	  - Code reads, file exploration, "show me X" requests.
67	  - One-off debugging that resolved within the turn.
68	  - Tool calls and their outputs (mechanics, not facts).
69	  - Restatements of things already in code, seed context, or git history.
70	  - "thanks" / "ok" / "keep going" / feedback that applies only to this turn.
71	
72	## Output Format
73	
74	When — and only when — you have a fact that passes all four checks, output ONE
75	line per fact in exactly this format:
76	
77	    <kind><TAB><taxonomy-path>[,<taxonomy-path>]<TAB><fact>
78	
79	The leading <kind> is exactly ONE of these six words — the *shape* of the claim,
80	independent of its topic:
81	
82	  - decision        — a resolved choice and its rationale (why X over Y)
83	  - invariant       — a rule that must always hold; a hard constraint
84	  - gotcha          — a non-obvious trap, footgun, or surprising behavior
85	  - preference      — how the user likes work done (style, tooling taste)
86	  - convention      — a standing process or formatting norm
87	  - closed-negative — a question settled negatively: what was tried or
88	                      considered, why it failed or was rejected (evidence),
89	                      and when to revisit. Use this — not decision — whenever
90	                      the durable content is "do NOT go down this path".
91	
92	${TAXONOMY_BLOCK}
93	
94	## Rules
95	
96	- Output 0–6 lines. ZERO is the default and expected outcome. Prove a fact earns
97	  its slot before emitting it.
98	- Each line is exactly: kind<TAB>path<TAB>fact, using real tab characters. The
99	  kind is one of the six words above; if genuinely unsure of the kind, you may
100	  omit it and emit path<TAB>fact — it will be inferred.
101	- A closed-negative fact's text must carry all three parts in one statement:
102	  what was tried/considered, why it failed or was rejected, and the condition
103	  under which revisiting would make sense (e.g. "Query expansion was tried for
104	  fact recall and rejected: the early lift collapsed at n=121 (d=0.10, n.s.);
105	  revisit only with a new expansion model or a measured recall ceiling.").
106	- EXACTLY three levels: category.subcategory.type (e.g.
107	  preferences.coding.style). Each segment is lowercase letters, digits, and
108	  underscores only — NO hyphens, NO uppercase, NO spaces. Use "ci_cd" not
109	  "ci-cd". Each path must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*(\.[a-z0-9_]+){2}$ — lines that
110	  do not match are dropped.
111	- Multi-path lines: a single fact may be stored under at most TWO paths, joined
112	  by a comma with no spaces, only when it genuinely belongs to two distinct
113	  top-level categories. Never more than two.
114	- Prefer paths shown in the taxonomy block; invent a new three-level path under
115	  an existing top-level category only if nothing fits.
116	- Each fact is ONE complete, self-contained statement. Use third person when the
117	  fact is about the human.
118	- DURABLE only: preferences, project/tool choices, roles, resolved decisions,
119	  architectural intent, constraints likely relevant across sessions.
120	- EXCLUDE: ephemeral task state, today-only TODOs, tool-call mechanics, what the
121	  agent did this turn, anything already in code/seed/git history, restated
122	  obvious facts, chit-chat, feedback that applies only to this turn ("that
123	  worked", "a bit shorter"), and in-flight or deferred decisions. NOTE: a
124	  standing rule expressed AS feedback ("don't do X anymore", "from now on do Y")
125	  IS durable — capture it. The test is whether the rule applies to future turns.
126	- NO preamble, NO explanation, NO bullets or numbering, NO "no facts found"
127	  message — only kind<TAB>path<TAB>fact lines, or a completely empty response.

Recon done. Here's what the repo actually has:

**The prompt** is `templates/entire-brain-distill.md`, shipped in the binary and used as the system prompt by `entire brain distill`. It's already aggressively anti-spam on paper: "Your default answer is NOTHING", a four-check quality gate (durable / useful / not already known / worth writing down), and a hard cap of 0–6 lines. But — the cap is **per 48KB transcript chunk**, not per session. A long session becomes many chunks, each allowed up to 6 facts, each judged with no memory of what the other chunks emitted. That's almost certainly where ~88/session comes from, and it means the eval must score at session level, not chunk level.

**The existing `facts eval` tooling is for retrieval, not generation** — it measures which stored facts surface for a query (precision/recall/useful-per-1k across ranking arms). It doesn't judge whether distillation should have produced a fact at all. So your eval doesn't exist yet, but three pieces are directly reusable: the judge plumbing (same agent-invocation path as distill, with a verdict cache), the A/B comparison machinery (`facts_eval_compare.go` — paired t-tests with Holm correction, so "prompt B beats prompt A" comes with significance, not vibes), and the task-file conventions.

**Offline re-runs are cheap to sandbox.** `distill` supports `--session`, `--branch`, `--force`, `--agent/--model`, `--max-chunk-bytes`, and the brain directory resolves through `XDG_DATA_HOME` — the test suite already isolates stores exactly this way. So the loop is: scratch `XDG_DATA_HOME`, export transcripts there, run distill with prompt variant X, collect facts, score. One wrinkle: transcripts aren't sitting on disk right now (the manifest lists 272 but the files get materialized on export from git checkpoint refs), and `distill --dry-run --json` reports per-session byte/chunk counts — which is exactly how we'll pick your short golden-set sessions.

So the design flaw is now crisply stated: **the unit of extraction (48KB byte window) no longer matches the unit of meaning (checkpoint) or the unit of storage/sync (checkpoint anchor)**. And each window gets an independent 0–6 budget with no view of the others, so budgets multiply with transcript length instead of with work done.

Here's the shape I think you're describing, played back. Distillation becomes checkpoint-scoped: the input unit is a checkpoint's transcript slice (the turns since the previous checkpoint — one commit's worth of work). The budget attaches to the checkpoint, say at most 1–2 facts, and the budget is a **cap, not a quota** — zero stays the default and the expected outcome, otherwise we'll just invert the bug and mint 2 memories per trivial commit. Mechanically a big checkpoint slice may still need internal chunking to fit context, which suggests two stages: chunks propose candidates, then a per-checkpoint select pass sees all candidates together and keeps only the best 0–2. That select stage is the real structural fix — it's the "judge with full view" that today doesn't exist anywhere.

# Memory-generation eval loop — design

Status: draft for review. Lives in `.context` (no committed docs in this repo).

## Intent

Entire's brain distills session transcripts into durable facts ("memories").
The store for this repo holds ~24,500 facts from 272 sessions — about 88 per
session — against roughly 50 PRs of actual work. The distillation prompt
(`templates/entire-brain-distill.md`) demands the opposite: "your default
answer is NOTHING", a four-check quality gate, and a 0–6 line cap. The cap is
per 48KB transcript chunk (`factsMaxPerChunk = 6`, enforced in code), each
chunk is judged with no view of the others, so the budget multiplies with
transcript length instead of with work done.

We want an eval loop that measures memory-generation quality so that prompt
and pipeline changes are judged by a scoreboard, not vibes. The first consumer
of the loop is a planned restructure: checkpoint-scoped distillation with a
small per-checkpoint budget.

North star, stated by the owner: memories must be purposeful. Not creating a
memory is the default, correct outcome. Volume is a cost, not a sign of
coverage.

## Goals

1. A repeatable, offline eval that scores the current distillation pipeline on
   a fixed set of real sessions from this repo.
2. A human golden set: keep/kill verdicts from the owner on the facts the
   current prompt produces for ~10–15 short sessions.
3. An LLM judge calibrated against those verdicts (report agreement; judge is
   trusted only where agreement is demonstrated) so the loop re-runs cheaply
   on larger samples.
4. Metrics that separate the two failure modes:
   - per-fact precision — share of generated facts a future session in this
     repo would genuinely benefit from (verdict or judge);
   - volume — facts per session and facts per checkpoint;
   - redundancy — near-duplicate rate within one run's output.
5. A/B comparison between pipeline variants (prompt text, chunking strategy,
   budgets, models) with paired significance, reusing the Holm-corrected
   compare machinery in `internal/cli/facts_eval_compare.go`.
6. Baseline the current pipeline first; then run the checkpoint-scoped
   restructure as the first A/B experiment.

## Non-goals

- Retrieval quality. `entire brain facts eval` / `eval-gen` / arms already
  cover which stored facts surface for a query. This eval judges whether a
  fact should exist at all.
- Reconciliation/merge quality (proposal dedup across sessions). Out of scope
  for the first loop; the redundancy metric only looks within a run.
- Benchmarks for publication. Internal decision tool only (recorded
  constraint: prior mem0/LongMemEval numbers are not publishable).
- Changing the production pipeline in this project. The restructure is its own
  follow-on project, planned separately once the eval exists.

## Anti-goals

- A quota that inverts the bug: any design where "1–2 per checkpoint" becomes
  a floor. Zero must remain the expected outcome for most checkpoints, and the
  eval must be able to detect quota-inversion (e.g. volume distribution
  clustered at the cap).
- An eval so heavy nobody re-runs it. One command, resumable, judge verdicts
  cached.
- Golden-set labeling that takes the owner more than a couple of hours total.

## Constraints

- Eval artifacts (task sets, run outputs, judge caches, labels) live in
  `~/.entire-brain-eval/`, not `/tmp` (recorded convention after a reboot lost
  a capstone's artifacts).
- Sandboxed runs: the brain directory resolves through `XDG_DATA_HOME`; eval
  runs point it at a scratch dir so nothing writes to the real store. The test
  suite already isolates stores this way.
- Transcripts are not sitting on disk; they are materialized by brain
  export/refresh from checkpoint data. The harness must export into the
  sandbox before distilling. `distill --dry-run --json` reports per-session
  bytes/chunks and is the session-picker for the golden set.
- Distillation agents are `codex`, `claude-code`, or `ollama` via
  `distillAgentCommandArgs`; the eval must pin one agent+model per run and
  record it in the run metadata, since results are agent-dependent (recorded:
  Gemma 4 12B local vs Claude Code differ materially in both speed and
  Claude-judged precision).
- Plain technical writing in all artifacts and labels UI.
- No committed docs; this design and run reports stay in `.context` /
  `~/.entire-brain-eval/` / Linear.

## Decided design

### Pipeline under test

One eval "system under test" = (prompt template, chunking strategy,
per-unit budget, agent, model). The current production configuration
(byte-chunked 48KB, 0–6 per chunk, shipped template) is variant A / the
baseline. Variants change one axis at a time where practical.

### Corpus and golden set

- Corpus: sessions already captured for this repo (272 in the manifest),
  selected by `distill --dry-run --json` stats. Fixed once and versioned in
  `~/.entire-brain-eval/` so every variant runs on identical input.
- Golden subset: ~10–15 short sessions (small byte size, few chunks, ideally
  ≥1 checkpoint). For each, the owner sees every fact the baseline produced,
  with enough session context to judge, and marks keep/kill (optional short
  reason). Verdict labeling only — no from-scratch authoring. This measures
  precision and spam; it cannot measure recall (accepted tradeoff, chosen by
  the owner).
- Labels are stored as a simple JSONL file (fact id/text, session id,
  checkpoint id, verdict, reason) in `~/.entire-brain-eval/`.

### Judge

- Same agent-invocation path as distill (reuse `distillAgentCommandArgs` and
  the judge-cache pattern from `eval-gen --refine`).
- Judge prompt asks the four-check question from the distill template against
  the fact plus its source context: would a future session in this repo
  genuinely benefit, is it durable, is it already discoverable, is it worth
  writing down. Binary verdict with a one-line reason.
- Calibration: run the judge over the golden-labeled facts, report agreement
  (plus per-class: agreement on owner-kills matters most, since spam is the
  concern). If agreement is poor, iterate on the judge prompt before trusting
  judge-scored runs; golden verdicts always override judge verdicts where both
  exist.

### Metrics per run

- precision: kept / total (golden where available, judge elsewhere; report
  the label source split, following the proof-vs-silver convention the
  retrieval eval already uses).
- facts per session and facts per checkpoint: mean and distribution; flag
  cap-clustering (quota inversion).
- redundancy: near-duplicate pairs within the run's output (method left to
  builder; candidates: the existing BM25 ranker self-similarity, or
  `factmerge` identity plus a fuzzy text threshold).
- cost: agent calls, tokens, wall time (reuse `--call-trace`).

### Comparison

- Paired per-session metrics across variants on the shared corpus, run
  through the existing Holm-corrected compare logic
  (`compareEvalSummaries`-style) so "B beats A" carries significance.

### Harness shape

- A hidden subcommand in the `facts eval` family (exact name and flag surface
  left to builder), so it ships with the binary like the retrieval eval does,
  plus whatever thin scripting in `~/.entire-brain-eval/` is needed for the
  labeling flow.
- Run flow: create scratch `XDG_DATA_HOME` → export/refresh the corpus
  sessions into it → run distill with the variant's configuration → collect
  fact records with provenance → score → write a run summary JSON.
- Prompt variants: the template is compiled into the binary; the harness
  needs an override hook (flag or env var pointing at an alternate template
  file). If no such hook exists, adding one is in scope for the harness.

### First experiment after baseline (scoped here, built later)

Checkpoint-scoped distillation: input unit is a checkpoint's transcript slice
(turns since the previous checkpoint), aligning extraction with the provenance
anchor and sync unit from Memories v3 (facts keyed by session + checkpoint +
commit, pushed on the post-commit event). Budget attaches to the checkpoint:
at most 1–2 facts, cap not quota. Oversized checkpoint slices still chunk
internally to fit context, but chunks only propose candidates; a per-checkpoint
select pass sees all candidates together and keeps the best 0–2. The eval
loop is the referee: the restructure must beat the baseline on precision and
volume without a redundancy or cost regression.

## Left to the builder

- Exact CLI surface (command name, flags) and run-summary schema.
- Labeling UX (likely: generate a markdown or JSONL sheet the owner edits;
  no interactive UI needed).
- Near-duplicate detection method for the redundancy metric.
- Judge prompt wording and the agreement threshold that gates judge-scored
  claims.
- How session export into the sandbox store works mechanically (refresh vs a
  narrower export path) — verify against current source; this design was
  written against commit 318e4b05.
- Corpus size for judge-scored runs (big enough for the paired tests to have
  power; the compare machinery reports n).

## Open questions for the owner

- Which agent+model is the canonical production distiller to pin the baseline
  to (claude-code with a specific model, codex, or must the eval cover
  several)?

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

# Memory-Generation Eval Loop Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** An offline, sandboxed eval that scores distillation (memory generation) quality — precision, volume, redundancy, cost — on real sessions, with golden human labels, a calibrated LLM judge, and paired A/B comparison between pipeline variants.

**Architecture:** Three small hooks go into the existing `distill` path (template override, per-chunk cap override, raw-extraction JSONL output that bypasses reconcile). A new hidden `entire brain facts distill-eval` command family orchestrates: build a fixed corpus, run distill variants in a scratch `XDG_DATA_HOME` sandbox by shelling out to the current binary, score the raw output, and compare runs with the existing paired-t/Holm primitives.

**Tech Stack:** Go, cobra, package `internal/cli` conventions (table tests, `httptest` loopback fake agents as in `TestDistillCommandOllamaLoopbackProducesTimedSummary`).

**Spec:** `.context/2026-10-23-memory-generation-eval-loop-design.md` (travels with this plan; executors read both).

## Global Constraints

- Eval artifacts live under `~/.entire-brain-eval/<run-name>/`, never `/tmp`.
- Sandboxing: every agent-invoking eval run uses a scratch `XDG_DATA_HOME`; the real brain store must never be written.
- Score RAW extraction output, pre-reconcile. Reconcile never runs in eval mode.
- Baseline pin: distiller `--agent claude-code --model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`. Judge: `claude-code --model claude-fable-5`, fixed per experiment, never the distiller under test.
- All new commands/flags are `Hidden: true`, like the existing `facts eval` family.
- Zero facts is a valid, expected outcome everywhere: no divide-by-zero, no dropped sessions.
- Run `oxfmt` CI check before any push; stage files by explicit name.
- Plain technical writing in all output and artifacts; no committed docs (plan/spec stay in `.context`).

## Review Focus

1. Judge output unparseable or truncated → facts default to NOT useful (never inflate precision). Test pinned in Task 5.
2. Session whose run produced zero facts → present in per-session results with `facts=0` and included in paired volume. Test pinned in Task 6.
3. Label sheet with a bad verdict (`"Keep"`, `"kil"`, empty) → import fails with the line number; never silently skipped. Test pinned in Task 4.
4. Template override path missing or lacking `${TAXONOMY_BLOCK}` → distill fails fast with a clear error; never silently falls back to the embedded template. Test pinned in Task 1.
5. Comparing summaries from different corpora or different judge configs → `compare` refuses unless an explicit `--allow-*` flag is passed. Test pinned in Task 7.

---

### Task 1: Distill hooks — template and cap overrides

**Files:**
- Modify: `internal/cli/distill.go` (`distillTemplate()`, ~line 55)
- Modify: `internal/cli/facts.go:24` area (cap accessor)
- Modify: `internal/cli/distill.go:285,321` (cap uses)
- Test: `internal/cli/distill_eval_hooks_test.go` (new)

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `entirebrain.Templates`, `stripTemplateFrontmatter`.
- Produces: env hooks `ENTIRE_BRAIN_DISTILL_TEMPLATE` (path to alternate template file) and `ENTIRE_BRAIN_FACTS_MAX_PER_CHUNK` (positive int); `func factsMaxPerChunkValue() int` replacing direct const reads in `distilledFactsFromOutput`.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write failing tests**

```go
func TestDistillTemplateEnvOverride(t *testing.T)        // env set to temp file with frontmatter+marker → body returned, frontmatter stripped
func TestDistillTemplateEnvOverrideMissingFile(t *testing.T) // env set to nonexistent path → error naming the path; NOT the embedded template
func TestRenderDistillPromptOverrideWithoutMarker(t *testing.T) // override file lacking ${TAXONOMY_BLOCK} → renderDistillPrompt errors
func TestFactsMaxPerChunkEnvOverride(t *testing.T)       // env "2" → distilledFactsFromOutput caps at 2 with the cap warning; env unset → 6; env "0"/"x" → error or default-with-warning? Pin: invalid value is an ERROR from factsMaxPerChunkValue's caller at distill startup, not a silent default
```

For the cap test, reuse the fixture style of `distill_test.go:313` (N+4 valid lines in, expect cap).

- [ ] **Step 2: Run tests, verify they fail** — `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestDistillTemplate|TestFactsMaxPerChunk|TestRenderDistillPromptOverride' -v`
- [ ] **Step 3: Implement.** `distillTemplate()` reads the env path when set (`os.ReadFile`, then `stripTemplateFrontmatter`). Add `factsMaxPerChunkValue() int` beside the const; `distilledFactsFromOutput` and its warning use it. Validate the cap env once at distill startup (in `runDistill` options resolution) so a bad value fails the command, not each chunk. Cache-salt rule: when either env override is active, append its value to the inputs of `distillCacheSalt` so cached chunks cannot leak across variants; when both are unset the salt inputs are byte-identical to today (production caches stay valid).
- [ ] **Step 4: Run tests, verify pass** — same command, expect PASS.
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit** — `git add internal/cli/distill.go internal/cli/facts.go internal/cli/distill_eval_hooks_test.go && git commit -m "feat(distill): env hooks for template and per-chunk cap overrides"`

### Task 2: Raw-extraction output mode on distill

**Files:**
- Modify: `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go` (`newDistillCommand` flags; `runDistillForBrain` lines ~977–1601)
- Test: `internal/cli/distill_raw_out_test.go` (new)

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: extraction loop in `runDistillForBrain` (records staged per branch before `reconcileBranch`), `factRecord`, `factAnchor`.
- Produces: hidden flag `--raw-facts-out <path>`. Semantics: extraction-only mode — no reconcile (neither mid-run nor end-of-run `reconcileBranch`), no store writes, no distill-cache fingerprint updates; extraction results stream to `<path>` as JSONL and the command exits after the extraction pool drains. Two line types:

```json
{"type":"chunk","session_id":"…","branch":"…","chunk_index":1,"chunk_count":3,"facts_emitted":6,"cap":6}
{"type":"fact","session_id":"…","branch":"…","chunk_index":1,"fact_id":"…","kind":"gotcha","paths":["a.b.c"],"text":"…","checkpoint_id":"…"}
```

`fact_id` is the existing content-derived `factRecordID`; `checkpoint_id` from the chunk's `factAnchor` (heuristic — downstream must not trust it for per-checkpoint attribution).

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test.** Model on `TestDistillCommandOllamaLoopbackProducesTimedSummary` (fake loopback ollama returning fixed fact lines):

```go
func TestDistillRawFactsOutSkipsReconcileAndStore(t *testing.T)
// run distill --raw-facts-out over a 2-chunk fixture session:
//   - output file has 2 chunk lines + expected fact lines with correct session_id/chunk_index
//   - fact store in the (test-sandboxed) brain dir gained NO facts
//   - summary/source reports ReconcileCalls == 0
//   - re-running distill afterward re-processes the session (no fingerprint was cached)
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run, verify FAIL** — `go test ./internal/cli -run TestDistillRawFactsOut -v`
- [ ] **Step 3: Implement** the flag (hidden), the JSONL writer (flushed per chunk so a crashed run keeps partial output), and the three skips. Branch early where records would be staged for reconcile.
- [ ] **Step 4: Run, verify PASS.**
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit** — `git add internal/cli/distill_cmd.go internal/cli/distill_raw_out_test.go && git commit -m "feat(distill): --raw-facts-out extraction-only JSONL mode"`

### Task 3: Corpus builder and sandboxed runner

**Files:**
- Create: `internal/cli/facts_distill_eval.go` (command tree + shared types)
- Create: `internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_run.go` (sandbox orchestration)
- Modify: `internal/cli/facts_admin_cmd.go:27-29` area (register `newFactsDistillEvalCommand(opts)`)
- Test: `internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_run_test.go` (new)

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: Task 1 env hooks, Task 2 `--raw-facts-out`; `entire brain refresh sessions`; `distill --dry-run --json` (per-session `chunks`, `raw_bytes` in `distillDryRunSession`).
- Produces: hidden command `entire brain facts distill-eval` with subcommands `corpus` and `run`.

```go
type distillEvalCorpus struct {
    RepoKey      string                   `json:"repo_key"`
    CreatedAt    time.Time                `json:"created_at"`
    CorpusSHA256 string                   `json:"corpus_sha256"` // sha256 of sorted session ids
    Sessions     []distillEvalCorpusEntry `json:"sessions"`
}
type distillEvalCorpusEntry struct {
    SessionID string `json:"session_id"`
    Branch    string `json:"branch"`
    RawBytes  int    `json:"raw_bytes"`
    Chunks    int    `json:"chunks"`
    Golden    bool   `json:"golden"`
}
type distillEvalRunMeta struct { // written as run.json next to raw-facts.jsonl
    Variant      distillEvalVariant `json:"variant"`
    CorpusSHA256 string             `json:"corpus_sha256"`
    StartedAt    time.Time          `json:"started_at"`
    WallSeconds  float64            `json:"wall_seconds"`
}
type distillEvalVariant struct {
    Name           string `json:"name"`
    TemplateSHA256 string `json:"template_sha256"` // sha of rendered template body actually used
    Agent          string `json:"agent"`
    Model          string `json:"model"`
    MaxChunkBytes  int    `json:"max_chunk_bytes"`
    CapPerChunk    int    `json:"cap_per_chunk"`
}
```

Command behavior to pin:
- `distill-eval corpus --out <dir> --sessions 60 --golden 12`: creates scratch `XDG_DATA_HOME` under `<dir>/sandbox`, shells out (via `os.Executable()`, `cmd.Env` with overridden `XDG_DATA_HOME`, cwd = repo root) to `brain refresh sessions`, then `brain distill --dry-run --json`; selects the `--sessions` smallest-by-`raw_bytes` sessions with `chunks >= 1`, marks the `--golden` smallest of those `Golden: true`; writes `<dir>/corpus.json`. Default `<dir>` is `~/.entire-brain-eval/<repo-key-slug>/`.
- `distill-eval run --corpus <corpus.json> --name <variant> [--template <file>] [--cap N] [--agent claude-code] [--model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001] [--max-chunk-bytes N] [--golden-only]`: fresh scratch `XDG_DATA_HOME` per run under `<corpus-dir>/runs/<name>/sandbox`; `refresh sessions`; then one `brain distill --session <id> --raw-facts-out … --call-trace … --agent … --model …` per corpus session (sequential; `--golden-only` restricts to golden entries), with Task 1 env vars set from `--template`/`--cap`; concatenated raw facts land in `<corpus-dir>/runs/<name>/raw-facts.jsonl`, call traces in `call-trace.jsonl`, metadata in `run.json`.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write failing tests** (use the package's XDG-sandboxed test home; fake agent = loopback ollama as in Task 2):

```go
func TestDistillEvalCorpusSelectsSmallestSessions(t *testing.T) // 3 fixture sessions of different sizes, --sessions 2 --golden 1 → 2 smallest picked, smallest is golden, corpus_sha256 = sha256 of sorted ids
func TestDistillEvalRunProducesArtifactsInSandbox(t *testing.T) // run over fixture corpus → raw-facts.jsonl + run.json exist; run.json carries variant fields incl. template_sha256 and cap; child process env contained the scratch XDG_DATA_HOME (assert via recorded cmd.Env or by the sandbox store being the one populated)
func TestDistillEvalRunRefusesWithoutCorpus(t *testing.T)       // missing corpus file → error naming the path
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run, verify FAIL** — `go test ./internal/cli -run TestDistillEvalCorpus\|TestDistillEvalRun -v`
- [ ] **Step 3: Implement.** Shell-out runner as a small `func(ctx, env, args…) (stdout []byte, err error)` seam so tests can intercept. Verify `refresh sessions` exports transcripts into the scratch brain dir (`sessions/<branch>/*.jsonl`); if its flag surface differs from the assumption, adapt here and note it in the commit message.
- [ ] **Step 4: Run, verify PASS.**
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit** — `git add internal/cli/facts_distill_eval.go internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_run.go internal/cli/facts_admin_cmd.go internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_run_test.go && git commit -m "feat(facts): distill-eval corpus and sandboxed run commands"`

### Task 4: Golden label sheet — generate and load

**Files:**
- Create: `internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_labels.go`
- Test: `internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_labels_test.go`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `raw-facts.jsonl` fact lines (Task 2 schema), corpus golden flags (Task 3).
- Produces: `distill-eval labels --run <run-dir> --corpus <corpus.json> --out labels.jsonl` → one line per fact from golden sessions, `verdict` empty for the owner to fill with `keep` or `kill`:

```json
{"fact_id":"…","session_id":"…","transcript_path":"…","kind":"gotcha","paths":["a.b.c"],"text":"…","verdict":"","reason":""}
```

and `func loadDistillEvalLabels(path string) (map[string]distillEvalVerdict, error)` where `distillEvalVerdict` is `{Verdict string // "keep"|"kill"; Reason string}` keyed by `fact_id`. Loader rejects any line whose verdict is not exactly `keep` or `kill` (case-sensitive), reporting the 1-based line number; a generated-but-unfilled sheet therefore fails loudly until fully labeled.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write failing tests**

```go
func TestDistillEvalLabelsSheetCoversGoldenFactsOnly(t *testing.T)
func TestLoadDistillEvalLabelsRejectsBadVerdict(t *testing.T) // verdicts "Keep", "kil", "" → error containing "line N"
func TestLoadDistillEvalLabelsRoundTrip(t *testing.T)
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run, verify FAIL** — `go test ./internal/cli -run DistillEvalLabels -v`
- [ ] **Step 3: Implement.**
- [ ] **Step 4: Run, verify PASS.**
- [ ] **Step 5: Commit** — `git add internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_labels.go internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_labels_test.go && git commit -m "feat(facts): distill-eval golden label sheet"`

### Task 5: Generation judge and calibration

**Files:**
- Create: `internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_judge.go`
- Test: `internal/cli/facts_distill_eval_judge_test.go`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: `distillAgentCommandArgs` + `injectAgentModel` (agent invocation), `judgeCache` (`facts_eval.go:489`) persistence pattern, raw fact lines, labels loader (Task 4).
- Produces:
  - `func distillEvalJudgePrompt() string` — a NEW prompt (do not reuse the retrieval `judgePrompt()`): given facts from one session, apply the distill template's four checks (durable / useful to a future session / not already discoverable / worth writing down) and answer `<fact#> keep|kill` per fact, one line each, no prose.
  - `distill-eval judge --run <run-dir> --agent claude-code --model claude-fable-5 --judge-cache <path> --out judge.jsonl` → `{"fact_id":"…","verdict":"keep"|"kill","judge_agent":"claude-code","judge_model":"claude-fable-5"}` per fact, batched per session. Unparseable/missing judge lines → `kill` (never inflate precision).
  - `distill-eval calibrate --labels labels.jsonl --judge judge.jsonl` → prints and writes `calibration.json`: `{ "n": N, "agreement": x, "agreement_on_kills": y, "agreement_on_keeps": z }` over facts present in both files.

- [ ] **Step 1: Write failing tests** (fake runner returning canned judge output; no real agent):

```go

# Executing Plans

Execute the plan yourself, task by task, in this session: no implementer
subagent per task, no reviewer per task. One fresh-context review of the
whole branch at the end.

**Why inline:** Subagent-driven development pays for a fresh implementer
and a fresh reviewer on every task, each re-reading the codebase from zero.
Inline execution pays for one context (yours) plus one reviewer at the end.
What it gives up is a fresh context per task and a second pair of eyes per
task. This skill keeps what those two things bought, by other means: the
brief is the spec, the ledger is your memory, TDD is the per-task gate, and
the final reviewer is the second pair of eyes.

**Core principle:** The plan already did the thinking. Execute it exactly,
prove each step with a test you watched fail and then pass, and leave a
record that survives your own forgetting.

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner
between tasks. They chose inline execution to spend less, not to answer
"should I continue?" after every task. Execute all tasks from the plan
without stopping.

**Rulings, not stalls.** Conflicts, ambiguities, plan defects — decide them.
The spec is the binding authority, the plan is its argument, and your
judgment settles what neither answers. Record every decision in the ledger
as `Ruling: <what you decided> — <why> — <what it costs if wrong>`, and keep
going. Deviating from the plan without a ledgered ruling is a decision made
in secret.

Four things stop you, and only these: an irreversible or destructive
operation; a security-sensitive action; a side effect outside this worktree
that norms say you ask about first (a merge, a push to a shared branch, a
publish); and a plan so broken that every path forward is a guess. For
those, stop and ask.

## When to Use

- You have a plan from superpowers:writing-plans and your human partner
  chose inline execution at the handoff.
- Your harness has no subagent tool (see the per-platform references in
  `../using-superpowers/references/`). Never fabricate a dispatch; run
  the plan here.
- Tasks are mostly independent — the same precondition as
  superpowers:subagent-driven-development.

A fully specified plan makes inline execution transcription plus testing:
it runs well on a mid-tier session model, and the one place the most
capable model earns its cost is the final review, which this skill
dispatches separately. Tell your human partner so when they choose inline.

Prefer superpowers:subagent-driven-development when your human partner
wants a review gate on every task, or when the plan is long enough that
its later tasks would run on a compacted context. Inline execution over a
long plan still works — the ledger is what makes it recoverable — but the
last tasks get the least of you.

## The Process

## Setup

Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. An inline executor that
loses its place re-implements tasks whose commits already exist — the same
failure as a controller re-dispatching them, paid for in your own context.
Track progress in a ledger file, not only in todos. Harness todos are a
live view; the ledger is the record.

The workspace and ledger are shared with superpowers:subagent-driven-development
— same directory, same format — so a plan can change executors mid-flight
and the new one resumes from the same ledger.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run
  `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it
  prints the plan's git-ignored directory
  (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to every
  artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, review packages. Another plan's
  directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are
  DONE — do not redo them; resume at the first task without one. Their
  commits exist in git even when your context no longer remembers making
  them: after compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own
  recollection. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file is
  another plan's progress: leave it and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch);
  if that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task. If the plan names a Spec, read that too: the spec is the
authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve
against it. A plan with no reachable spec gets a ledger note saying so —
rulings made without one are provisional.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** load superpowers:test-driven-development now,
before Task 1. It governs every step of every task below; a plan whose
steps already say "write the failing test first" does not exempt you
from reading it.

Before Task 1, scan the plan for conflicts between tasks. The plan's
Interfaces blocks tell you where to look: for every task that consumes
what an earlier task produces, one ledger row — the two tasks, what one
produces against what the other consumes, and what you found. Tasks that
share nothing get no row; a plan whose tasks share nothing gets the single
line `Pre-flight: no shared interfaces`. Rule on each conflict a row
surfaces with the spec as the binding authority, record the ruling beside
its row, and start Task 1. Each task's own text is checked when you read
its brief, not here.

## The Task Loop

Everything you print, and every tool result, stays resident in your
context for the rest of the session. Redirect long test output to a file
in the workspace and read its tail; read a brief, not the whole plan.

### 1. Take the task

- Run this skill's `scripts/task-start PLAN_FILE N`. It prints the brief
  path and BASE (the commit the task's range is cut from) in one call.
  Read the brief for every task, including ones you remember from setup:
  what you remember is a summary, the brief has the exact values,
  signatures, and test cases.
- Mark the task's todo in_progress.

Every tool call is a turn that re-reads your whole context. Bookkeeping
rides along with work — a ledger append in the same call as the commit,
never in a call of its own.

### 2. Work the steps

The plan's steps are already in RED-GREEN order; follow them in that
order under superpowers:test-driven-development, loaded at setup. A test
step's code is written first and run first. Watching it fail is a step,
not a formality — a test that passes before the implementation exists is
a finding about the test.

Every step that runs a command has an `Expected:` line. Run the command,
read its output, and compare. Three outcomes:

- **Matches.** Next step.
- **The code is wrong.** Use superpowers:systematic-debugging. Find the
  cause; never patch the symptom to make the step's output match.
- **The plan is wrong** — a step contradicts the spec, an interface from an
  earlier task doesn't match what this task consumes, a command that
  cannot work. Rule on the smallest change that satisfies the spec, ledger
  it as `Task <N>: Ruling: <finding> — <what you decided and why>`, and
  continue. The ruling is carried, not remembered: later tasks that touch
  the same interface read it from the ledger.

Commit as the plan's commit steps say. A task that spans several commits
is fine; BASE is what the review range is cut from, never `HEAD~1`.

### 3. The completion contract

Before a task's ledger line, all of the following are true, with evidence
in this session — not inferred from the diff looking right:

- Every test the brief names exists and ran in this task, and you read
  the output.
- The final test run for the task passed — `task-done` is that run, and
  it writes the command and result into the ledger line.
- Every `Expected:` line in the brief was compared against real output.
- Every deviation from the brief has a `Ruling:` line in the ledger.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** superpowers:verification-before-completion governs
the claim. If any item is missing, the task is not complete: finish it.

### 4. Complete the task

Run this skill's `scripts/task-done PLAN_FILE N BASE -- <test command>`
with the test command the brief names for the whole task. It runs the
tests, keeps the full output in the workspace, prints the tail, and — only
if they pass — appends the completion line to the ledger:

`Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, tests: <command> → <result>)`

A failing run records nothing; the task is not complete. When it records,
mark the todo complete and take the next task.

## Final Review

Run `../subagent-driven-development/scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`
(MERGE_BASE = the commit the branch started from, e.g.
`git merge-base main HEAD`) and review from the file it prints.

**With a subagent tool:** dispatch the reviewer on the most capable
available model — the whole-branch review is a judgment task — using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md), with the
package path, the plan and spec paths, the plan's Review Focus section
verbatim if it has one (the input classes and failure modes the plan's
tests do not exercise — the reviewer checks each deliberately), and a
pointer to the ledger's `Ruling:` lines so it can weigh the calls you
made. Specify the model
explicitly; an omitted model inherits the session's, which may not be the
most capable. This is the one fresh context the whole run buys. Do not
skip it, and do not replace it with your own read of the diff.

**Without a subagent tool:** read code-reviewer.md and perform that review
yourself against the package, as a separate pass after the last task's
ledger line. Write `Final review: self-review (no subagent tool)` to the
ledger, and say so in your final message: a self-review by the author is
weaker than a fresh reviewer, and your human partner decides whether that
is enough before merge.

Sort the findings before you act on any of them. The reviewer's severity
labels are advice; the gate is yours. Its "Declined to judge" list is
yours too: every line there is a ruling you make and ledger, exactly like
a plan conflict — `Final: Ruling: <behavior the reviewer set aside> —
<what a reasonable person using this software gets, and why that stands
or why it is now a finding> — <cost if wrong>`. Re-grade first, by effect: the
spec is a vision document, and a finding's grade is what a reasonable
person using this software gets if it ships, not whether the spec names
the input that triggers it — a reviewer who set a finding at Minor
because the spec was silent has graded the spec, not the effect. Then:

- **Critical and Important** enter the fix pass.
- **Minor** goes to the ledger as `Final: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`
  and to your final message under "Deferred minors". Minors never enter
  the fix pass, and never become rulings — a ruling is a decision about a
  conflict, not a note that you declined a polish suggestion.

Fix the Critical and Important findings yourself — you are the
implementer here — in ONE pass. Each fix is verified by TDD, not by a
second reviewer: write the test that reproduces the finding, watch it
fail, make it pass, then run the whole suite. Record each in the ledger as
`Final: fixed <finding> — <test name> RED→GREEN, suite <N>/<N>`. A fix
without a test that failed first is not verified; a suite that is not
green after the pass means the pass is not over. Do not dispatch a
re-review: it would re-read a diff whose covering tests already answer
"addressed" and whose suite run already answers "broke nothing".

A finding you decide not to fix is a ruling — `Final: Ruling: <finding> —
<why the code stands> — <cost if wrong>` — and reaches your human partner
in the rulings list. There is no second fix pass.

## Finish

Before you delete anything, collect every ledger line containing
`Ruling:` into your final message under "Rulings I made", in the order you
made them, each with what it costs if wrong, and every `minor (deferred)`
line under "Deferred minors". Both lists are exhaustive. Your final
message is the only place the decisions you took on your human partner's
behalf — and the findings you chose not to act on — reach them.

When the final review is clean and its fixes are committed, delete this
plan's workspace directory — the git history is the record now. Sibling
directories belong to other plans; leave them alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I remember what Task N says" | You remember a summary. The brief has the exact values. Read it. |
| "The plan's code is right, skip watching the test fail" | A test you never saw fail proves nothing. It is one step. Run it. |
| "I'll run the full suite at the end instead of per step" | Per-step runs are how you learn which step broke it. The end-of-task run is the contract, not a substitute. |
| "The plan is wrong here, I'll just do the right thing" | Do the right thing and ledger the ruling. Unledgered deviation is a decision made in secret. |
| "I'll write the ledger lines after a few tasks" | Compaction does not wait for a convenient moment. One line per task, in the same message as the commit. |
| "Let me check in before the next task" | They chose inline to spend less. Progress prompts spend their time instead. Only the four stops stop you. |
| "I read my own diff carefully; the final reviewer is redundant" | Same author, same blind spots. The reviewer is the only fresh context this run buys. |
| "Tests should pass, the change was trivial" | "Should" is not evidence. The contract requires the command and its output. |
| "Subagents are slow and expensive, I'll skip the final review too" | Inline already removed the per-task reviewers. One review of the whole branch is the floor, not the ceiling. |
| "The reviewer said Minor, so it's Minor" | The label graded the spec's silence. Grade what the person gets. Re-grade, then gate. |
| "The fix is obvious, no need for a failing test first" | The failing test is the only proof the finding was real and is now gone. Without it you have a diff and a hope. |
| "I'll fix the minors too while I'm in there" | Every minor you fix is a test, a fix, and a suite run your partner did not ask for. Ledger them; your partner decides. |

## Example Workflow

```

[Setup: worktree verified]
